title: Wonders are many
author: Sophocles
lines: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
Over the surging sea, with a whitening south wind wan,
Through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way;
And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
Ever he furrows and scores, as his team, year in year out,
With breed of the yoked horse, the ploughshare turneth about.
Speech and the wind-swift speed of counsel and civic wit,
He hath learnt for himself all these; and the arrowy rain to fly
And the nipping airs that freeze, ’neath the open winter sky.
He hath provision for all: fell plague he hath learnt to endure;
Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure.
why: The most famous chorus in Greek: human beings are the most wonderful and the most terrible thing in the world, masters of sea, earth and city, with a remedy for everything but death. Say it when you are proud of what people can do, and remember its last line.

title: Wisdom through suffering
src: Aeschylus, Agamemnon 176–183 · tr. E. D. A. Morshead (1881)
author: Aeschylus
lines: ’Tis Zeus alone who shows the perfect way
Of knowledge: He hath ruled,
Men shall learn wisdom, by affliction schooled.
In visions of the night, like dropping rain,
Descend the many memories of pain
Before the spirit’s sight: through tears and dole
Comes wisdom o’er the unwilling soul—
why: Aeschylus' hymn to Zeus: we learn by suffering, and wisdom comes even to the unwilling. Robert Kennedy quoted this passage (in another translation) on the night Martin Luther King was murdered. Say it in grief, not as an explanation, but as a hope that pain need not be wasted.

title: We must obey God rather than men
author: Acts
lines: But Peter and the apostles answered,
We must obey God rather than men.
why: Peter's answer to the council that ordered him to be silent: the motto of conscience from the martyrs to Thomas More and beyond. Say it when you are asked to do what you know is wrong.
